content.title: Lack of novelty
content.review:
This submission studies the problem setting of online incremental learning where individual data points are streamed online with nonstationarity and the algorithm is required to learn in one pass without revisiting the raw data. Techniques included in this work are "online bayesian learning", "memory/coreset replay" and "product quantization to compress the buffer".

### Pros:
1. The problem setting is more interesting than most previous works. Namely, one data at a time is a much more difficult setting than the other task incremental settings. As the sequence is much longer and forgetting is more of a problem.
2. The presentation is clear and very easy to follow.

### Cons:
1. The various methods used in this submission are not novel.
  - **streaming bayesian update**, is the technique used in various previous papers. Most of them are cited in this submission. A minor difference is the replacement of (8) & (9) into (6).
  - **memory-based**, is the same as coreset / replay-buffer.
  - **product-quantization**, is proposed in Heyes et al 2019 which is cited in this submission.
2. Methodwise I can't tell the difference between $\text{BASIL}$ and $\widehat{\text{VCL}}$. The difference lies in the way replay buffer is stored. This difference, however, is not novel as stated in 1.
3. It is not reasonable to store raw pixels for $\widehat{\text{VCL}}$. Since it is assumed that the pretrained convolution base net is available to all methods, it is more reasonable to store it in feature space without PQ. (If the feature vector is smaller than the original image, it is fairer to compare this way.) Nevertheless, despite this potentially unfair setting for VCL baseline, the major conclusion seems to be saying if we store the replay buffer in a PQ compressed way, and limit the memory size in megabyte, it will outperform storing the raw pixels. This feels trivial to me. Taking one step back, this has already been said in Hayes et al. 2019b.
4. This work doesn't compare with Hayes et al 2019b, the reason given is that Hayes et al doesn't use the streaming bayesian approach. I don't think this is a good reason because I doubt how much of the performance reported in this work comes from the streaming bayesian update. Sebastian et al. reported in [this paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.09733) that the bayesian part contributes marginally to the performance. Using only replay buffer achieves similar performance. As this work uses a replay buffer size of 10000 for CIFAR10/CIFAR100, it is not very surprising to me that the performance is much better than any baseline. I strongly doubt that the performance comes solely from the replay buffer. The streaming bayesian would only add a little margin if any. Having a comparison with Hayes et al could provide an answer to this question. However, it will not change my overall rating because of the reason stated in 3.
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: Limited Novelty, Poorly Designed Experiments
content.review:
## Summary
The paper extends Variational Continual Learning (VCL) (Nguyen et al., 2017) to a streaming learning setting.
The main novelties claimed by the authors are summarized as follows:
- Streaming learning setting: non-iid, online learning with batch size 1
- The use of pre-trained feature extractor
- Saving product-quantized features (instead of raw data) to the memory

---

## Pros

- The paper is easy to follow.

---

## Cons

### Using a pre-trained feature extractor

One of the main contributions of this paper is the use of a pre-trained feature extractor. In the experiments, the authors use Mobilenet-V2 pre-trained on Imagenet. However, there are two critical problems in this setting.

First, the lower layers of a CNN is transferable to other datasets only when the pre-trained dataset is sufficiently diverse. For instance, it is obvious that a CNN pre-trained on MNIST would not perform well on CIFAR10. Although this is an extreme example, novel low-level features, which are not captured by the pre-trained network, can generally appear in new datasets. And I think learning new features is one of the main goals of deep learning.

Second, training only the classifier network of Mobilenet-V2 is equivalent to training a logistic regression model. In Mobilenet-V2, only a linear layer remains if we exclude the convolutional layers. Therefore, the experiments are performed on a logistic regression model, not a deep neural network. I think the authors should have tested multi-layer architecture.


### Limited novelty
First, I am not convinced that the streaming learning setting is novel. Learning neural networks with streaming data has been proposed as in [1]. Also, there are continual learning methods that can be used with a batch size of 1, some of which do not require task ID [2].

Second, the differences between VCL and BaSIL are not significant. Compressing the features using product quantization and storing the features are engineering techniques that are far from algorithmic advancement. The core algorithm is identical to VCL. According to my understanding, the performance gap between VCL and BaSIL is due to the difference between the number of samples stored in memory (table 1). If the VCL could save the same number of examples, the score would be the same.

[1] Doyen Sahoo, Quang Pham, Jing Lu, Steven C. H. Hoi. Online Deep Learning: Learning Deep Neural Networks on the Fly. IJCAI 2018.

[2] Rahaf Aljundi, Klaas Kelchtermans, Tinne Tuytelaars. Task-Free Continual Learning. CVPR 2019.

### Other minor issues

- The memory update scheme in appendix A.2 will bias the memory towards newer samples. Using reservoir sampling can prevent such bias.
- Important experimental setting and results are missing in the main text, e.g., the classifier network's architecture, absolute accuracy values in Appendix B (at least Offline's score should be presented), etc.

---

## Overall evaluation

Overall, I think this paper does not present a novel and impactful idea. Moreover, the proposed method BaSIL and other baselines are tested only on a logistic regression model with a single linear layer. Therefore, I recommend rejection.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

display_title: Review of BaSIL, a new approach to perform online learning that combines BNNs and PQ compression of latent variables

content.title: Review of BaSIL, a new approach to perform online learning that combines BNNs and PQ compression of latent variables
content.review:
### Summary:

In this paper, the authors propose a new approach to perform streaming learning with BNNs while avoiding the issue of catastrophic forgetting, named BaSIL. This is done through the usage of a Bayesian approach, which represents a natural framework on which to do continual learning due to its basic formulation. Although it is more general in principle, the method is tested in image classification datasets, hence it consists of a CNN (only convolutional layers) chained to a BNN which takes the place of the regular fully-connected part of the CNNs. The system employs the CNN to encode the data into latent variables, which are then compressed using Product Quantization and stored in a small memory. This allows storing much more data than similar previous approaches, as well as efficient sampling in order to train the model when a new data instance arrives. The method is compared against other ones present in the literature, showing significant improvements in memory efficiency as well as in the final predictive results. 

#### Pros:

* The method seems well-motivated since the usage of the Bayesian approach allows for the type of updates that the predictive distributions would need in order to perform online learning. 
* The fact that the data stored is not the raw input, but rather a compressed version of the already smaller latent variables obtained after passing the data through the CNN seems like a smart way of preserving a lot of the original information using the least amount of memory possible. 
* Thanks to the good memory efficiency, the method is able to recall many more previous data points in comparison to the methods it is being compared against. Therefore, it is able to remember many more data points than previous approaches, and this in turn results in improved performance. 

#### Cons:

* The method depends on compressing the input data to the latent variables and then applying PQ to them to store them in memory. The final part of this procedure is done to each input, on which every latent vector is split into a number of smaller sub-vectors, which are then quantized using K-means. There seems to be a high dependency on the parameters of both the number of sub-vectors to decompose every latent representation, as well as the number of centroids chosen for each K-means. However, this issue is not addressed anywhere. Has there been any previous analysis on the influence both of these parameters have on the final results of the algorithm? Some type of systematic comparison for them could clarify this, f.e. performing cross-validation or some other type of test. 
* Another important parameter that is left uncommented is the final shape of the latent representation, which must influence greatly the rest of the remaining algorithm. Please comment on that and state whether any experiments have been conducted to address this. 
* The method here is only applied to image classification, but the approach seems to be more general. Have some other experiments been carried out with regression problems? For example, high-dimensional input data may be of interest. 
* In the experiments, the CNN convolutional layers are firstly trained using deterministic FC layers at the end. Once the convolutional layers are trained, the FC is replaced with the BNN to perform the streaming learning. How would the results change if the CNN was trained already with the BNN-fully-connected layers? And why not use a Bayesian CNN also? 
* Using projection operations seems to be a way of losing important information about the distribution of the parameters. How is this problem faced? Is there any way to quantify this?
* Having the prior and posterior distributions as Gaussian distributions (one mean-field and another a multivariate Gaussian) may seem restrictive. Here it seems to be a matter of having an easy form to evaluate the ELBO, but this restriction may lose important information when the data does not correspond to this assumption. Please address this and elaborate on the limitations that this emposes.

##### Other comments:

* It would be helpful to have an explicit expression for the KL divergence you use, f.e. including in the appendix the explicit expression for it in this case. 
* As an optional suggestion, when using a "blank" input to a function or distribution, I would choose to employ "\cdot" ($\cdot$) instead of "." since it is the more common notation (i.e. $F(\cdot)$ instead of $F(.)$). This is completely optional though. 
* The extra compression done by employing PQ is central here. However, why is it preferable to just having a small output on the CNN or something similar to what can be done in VAEs?
* Why are there only 16 samples in use at each moment? Since it seems to be efficient, why not employ more? 
* Regarding the refreshment of the memory where the compressed data is stored, why is it that you remove a random sample from memory? Why not consider it as a moving window and removing the oldest point in the memory?
* The graphs in the appendix are a good illustration of comparative performance. Another interesting way of comparing the methods would be relative to the baseline provided by offline learning, reporting the relative accuracy with respect to it.
* Correct from the text:
 - Section 2.1, line 5 - connect the two sentences, the period in "...data. It results..." seems to be out of place.
 - Section 2.3, after expression (1) - Remove comma after "Consider, ...". Add a comma after "Then" in the next sentence. Also, remove the "-" from the end of this sentence as well (in general, pay more attention to punctuation symbols all through the text).
 - Table 1 - at the end, "method" should be "methods".
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review:
This work applies online variational Bayes to image data that is pre-processed by a convolutional neural network (CNN) and a Vector-Quantization (VQ) technique.

Contribution / Novelty:
This work effectively applies VCL to pre-processed data, i.e. image data from which features have been extracted by a CNN and VQ. 
Thus, this work falls a bit short in novelty as it merely combines a online variational Bayesian approach with a learned feature extraction approach. Neither is novel; I do not see a scientific contribution here. The only 2 equations in the methods section (Eq. 6 and Eq. 7) are exactly what has been previously proposed in VCL.  

Clarity / Language:
The paper is easy to follow and written rather colloquially.
I would advise the authors to re-iterate the manuscript. For some paragraphs the purpose is not clear and should be more streamlined to focus on the relevant things only. For example, the catastrophic forgetting problem can be summarized in the introduction in a single sentence. 

Experimental Results:
The evaluation is limited to several quantitative results. While these are well done, some qualitative investigations (e.g. problems with baselines that are “solved” by this work) etc. should be included.

Related Work:
The related work section is missing / limited to the introduction. I would advise the authors to conduct a thorough literature research and relate to existing approaches.
For example, the authors may want to include alternative memory-based online variational Bayesian approaches such as [1] from ICLR 2020. 

[1] Continual Learning with Bayesian Neural Networks for Non-Stationary Data, ICLR 2020
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature
